title: On a curve of genus 1 every indecomposable rank 2 vector bundle of even degree is an extension of the form $ 0 \to M \rightarrow E \to M \to 0 $
text:
This is from Mukai's book on invariants and moduli spaces.

Proposition 10.48. On a curve of genus 1 every indecomposable rank 2 vector bundle of even degree is an extension of the form
$$
0 \rightarrow M \rightarrow E \rightarrow M \rightarrow 0
$$
for some line bundle $M$ on $C$.
Proof. It will be sufficient to consider the case $\operatorname{deg} E=2$. By Riemann-Roch, $h^{0}(E) \geq 2$, so that we can use two linearly independent sections $s, t \in H^{0}(E)$ to construct a homomorphism
$$
f: \mathcal{O}_{C} \oplus \mathcal{O}_{C} \rightarrow E, \quad(a, b) \mapsto a s+b t
$$
Claim: $f$ is injective.
Suppose not. Then the image is a subsheaf of rank 1 , and we denote its saturation by $L \subset E$. Then $\operatorname{deg} L \geq 2$ because $h^{0}(L) \geq 2$. But this contradicts Lemma 10.40. Since $\operatorname{deg} E=2$, the homomorphism $f$ cannot be surjective. In other words, there exists some point $p \in C$ at which the induced map $k \oplus k \rightarrow E / E(-p)$ fails to be an isomorphism. This means that $E$ contains $\mathcal{O}_{C}(p)$ as a subsheaf and, by Lemma 10.40, as a line subbundle. The quotient line bundle $M=E / \mathcal{O}_{C}(p)$ then has degree 1 . But indecomposability of $E$ implies that $H^{1}\left(M^{-1}(p)\right) \neq 0$, and hence $M$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{O}_{C}(p)$, proving the proposition.

For reference, Lemma 10.40 states that if $E$ is an indecomposable vector bundle of rank $2$, then every line subbundle $L \subset E$ satisﬁes $2\deg L \le \deg E + 2g -2$.
Mukai loses me after stating that $f$ cannot be surjective. I don't understand how the surjectivity of $f$ is equivalent to there existing a point $p \in C$ at which the induced map $k \oplus k \rightarrow E / E(-p)$ fails to be an isomorphism? I tried to search what on earth the notation $E(-p)$ is supposed to mean, but he does not state this in the book.

title: Analogous mean value theorem for Jordan curves
text:
Recently I came across the following theorem. Let $\Gamma$ be a Jordan curve and $F:\overline{int(\Gamma)} \to \mathbb{C}$ be continuous and analytic on $int(\Gamma))$. Then for each $z_0\in int(\Gamma)$ there exists two distinct points $z_1,z_2\in \Gamma$ such that
$$
F'(z_0) = \frac{F(z_2) - F(z_1)}{z_2-z_1}
$$
where by $int(\Gamma)$ is the unique bounded component of $\mathbb{C}\setminus \Gamma$. This theorem can be proved by employing the Osgood-Taylor-Caratheodory theorem, (and also an interesting/cool consequence is that every point inside the curve is the midpoint of some cord of the curve). In any case this is similar to the mean value theorem, and I was wondering if there is a similar theorem which would be precisely the mean value theorem. More precisely is it true that for any $z_1,z_2\in \Gamma$ there exists $z_0 \in int(\Gamma)$ so that,
$$
F'(z_0) = \frac{F(z_2) - F(z_1)}{z_2-z_1}
$$
or general is there some sort of mean value theorem (not property) for analytic functions. Thanks in advance.

title: Why can't Moore graphs contain cycles of length 3 or 4?
text:
We say a $k$-regular graph $G$ is a Moore graph if $G$ has diameter $2$ and $1+k^2$ vertices. Apparently the following is an equivalent definition if $k>1$:

A Moore graph is a $k$-regular graph such that for any distinct vertices $x$ and $y$, there is exactly one path of length at most $2$ between $x$ and $y$.

Why are these definitions equivalent? I can prove that the second definition implies the first (see below), but it's not clear to me why the first implies the second, i.e. why a Moore graph (using the first definition) does not contain a triangle or a 4-cycle.

Proof that the second definition implies the first:
The diameter can't be $1$ (else we get a complete graph, which contains triangles) so the diameter is $2$. Starting with any vertex $v$, the neighbors $v_1,\dots, v_k$ are non-adjacent (no triangles). Each $v_i$ is adjacent to $k-1$ more distinct vertices $v_{i,1}, \dots, v_{i, k-1}$, none of which are mutually adjacent. Now if $v_{i,p} = v_{j,q}$ for some $1\leq i,j\leq k$, $1\leq p,q\leq k-1$, we get a $4$-cycle $$ v\to v_i \to v_{i,p}=v_{j,q} \to v_j \to v$$ so in total we have at least $1+k+k(k-1)=1+k^2$ vertices.
Also, if $G$ has diameter 2, then $G = \{v\} \cup \Gamma(v)\cup \Gamma(\Gamma(v)) $ so $|G| \leq 1 + k + k(k-1)=k^2+1$.

title: Let $\ell_2=\{(x_n): \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n|^2\lt \infty\}$ and $A=\{(x_n):|x_n|\leq \frac 1n,n\in \Bbb N\}\subseteq\ell_2.$ Show that $A$ is closed.
text:
Let $\ell_2=\{(x_n)\subseteq \Bbb C: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n|^2\lt \infty\}$ and $A=\{(x_n):|x_n|\leq \frac 1n,n\in \Bbb N\}\subseteq X=\ell_2.$ Show that $A$ is closed.
My solution goes like this:
Let $x\in A'$, where $A'$ is the derived set of $A.$ This means, that $\exists$ a sequence $(x^{(k)})$ that converges to $x\in A',$ where $x^{(k)}=\{x_1^{(k)},x_2^{(k)},...\}$
So, for $\epsilon>0$ $\exists N\in\Bbb N$ such that $d(x^{(k)},y)<\epsilon,\forall k\geq N.$ Hence, $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}|x_i^{(k)}-x_i|^2\lt \epsilon,\forall k\geq N,\forall i\in \Bbb N.$
This implies, $|x_i^{(k)}-x_i|\lt\epsilon^{1/2}=\epsilon',\forall k\geq N,\forall i\in\Bbb N,$ which further implies $\lim_{k\to\infty}x_i^{(k)}=x_i,\forall i\in \Bbb N.$
Now, $|x_i^{(k)}|\leq \frac 1i,\forall k\in \Bbb N\implies |x_i^{(k)}|\leq \frac 1i,\forall k\in\Bbb N\implies \lim_{k\to\infty}|x_i^{(k)}|=|x_i|\leq \frac 1i,\forall i\in \Bbb N\implies x\in A.$ Thus, $A$ is closed.

Can the above solution be improved? Any suggestions on how make the above proof more readable will be highly appreciated. I want to specifically improve the proof writing in order to make the arguments more presentable. Lastly, if there is any mistake with my proof, please feel free to point it out.

title: Using the Martingale Representation Theorem to generalize the Geometric Brownian Motion
text:
I'm having trouble understanding the reasoning given in a proof of the following theorem in the book A First Course in Statistic Calculus by Louis-Pierre Arguin.

Theorem 7.26. Let $(M_t, t \in [0, T])$ be a continuous martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F_t}, t \leq T)$ with $M_0 = 0$ and with quadratic variation $\left\langle M \right\rangle_t = t$. Then $(M_t, t \leq T)$ is a standard Brownian motion.

The exposition is as follows:

The Martingale Representation Theorem implies that we can write $M_t = \int_{0}^{t} V_s \mathrm{d}B_s$ for some adapted process $(V_t, t \leq T)$. For simplicity, we assume that $V_s$ is such that the process (7.17) is a martingale.
7.17. (A generalization of geometric Brownian motion). Consider $(\int_{0}^{t}V_s \mathrm{d}B_s, t \geq 0)$ an Itô process. Define the positive process $M_t = \exp\bigg(\int_{0}^{t} V_s \mathrm{d}B_s - \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{t} V^2_s\mathrm{d}s\bigg), t \geq 0$
We show that the increments of $M$ are independent with the right distribution. In fact, we show that for $0 \leq s \lt t \leq T$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, we have:
${\bf E}[\exp(\lambda(M_t − M_s))|\mathcal{F}_s] = e^{\frac{\lambda^2}{2}(t-s)}$
Consider for $t \geq s$ the process:
$Y_t = \exp\bigg(\lambda(M_t - M_s) - \frac{\lambda^2}{2}\int_{s}^{t} V^2_u \mathrm{d}u\bigg) = \exp\bigg(\lambda\int_{s}^{t} V_u \mathrm{d}B_u - \frac{\lambda^2}{2}(t-s)\bigg)\tag{1}$
Note that $Y_s = 1$. As discussed in Example 7.17, this is a martingale. This implies:
$1 = {\bf E}\big[Y_t|\mathcal{F}_s] = {\bf E}[\exp(\lambda(M_t − M_s) −\frac{\lambda^2}{2}(t-s))|\mathcal{F}_s\big] \tag{2}$

In (1), how do we get to the last equality? Is it true that $\int_{s}^{t} V^2_u \mathrm{d}u = (t-s)$?
If so, can someone explain why and confirm whether (2) follows by taking the first term from the middle expression in (1) (implying $M_t - M_s = \int_{s}^{t} V_u \mathrm{d}B_u$) with the second term in final expression in (1)? Otherwise, can someone please fill me in on how we get the last expression in (1) and and then how we get (2)?

title: Recovering localizable measure from null sets of localizable measurable space.
text:
I have a problem with understanding how does the duality between categories of localizable measurable spaces and von Neumman algebras work.
To sum up:
A localizable measurable space is a measurable space $(X,\mathcal{A})$, equipped with a $\sigma-$ideal of null sets $\mathcal{I}$, such that for each family of measurable subsets, there exist its essential suppremum, that is a set in which each member of such family essentially contains. (by essentially contains I mean that for $E, F \in \mathcal{A},$ $E$ essentially contains $F$ if $\{x\in X: x \in F \land x \notin E\} \in \mathcal{I}$).
From what I know a localizable measurable space can admit only a localizable measure $\mu$. That is satisfying the following conditions:

For every $E \in \mathcal{A}$ with $\mu(E)>0,$ $E$ essentially contains $F \in \mathcal{A}$, such that $\mu(F) < \infty.$
For every family $\{E_j\}_{j \in J} \subset \mathcal{A},$ there exist $E \in \mathcal{A}$, such that $E$ essentially contains each $E_j$ and for any $F \in \mathcal{A}$, such that $F$ essentially contains each $E_j$, we have that $F$ essentially contains $E.$ (Set $E$ is called an essential union of $\{E_j\}_{j \in J}$).

A localizable measure spaces have all desired properties e. g. for such a space $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$ a topological dual $\big(L^1(X,\mathcal{A},\mu) \big)'$ is isomorphic as a Banach space to $L^\infty(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$ and also the Radon-Nikodym theorem holds.
Von Neumann algebras in this setting we understand not asbtractly: as a $*$-subalgebra $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}$ of a C*-algebra $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{H})$ of bounded linear operators on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ over a field of complex numbers $\mathbb{C},$ containing the identity operator $I$ and closed in weak operator topology.
By the results of Segal I think, we have a duality of the following categories

$\mathfrak{locmeas}$ - a category of localizable measurable spaces, where objects are localizable measurable spaces and morphism are classes of abstraction of measurable functions, considered up to null sets.
$\mathfrak{commvn}$ - a category of commutative von Neumann algebras, where objects are commutative von Neumann algebras and morphisms are $*-$homomorphism of a closed $*$-subalgebras of $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{H}),$ continuous in weak operator topology.

The functor acts by taking for a localizable measurable space $(X,\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{I})$ a space $L^\infty(X,\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{I})$. But here $L^\infty$ is considered as a multiplication operators on a Hilbert space $L^2.$ Norm on $L^\infty$ can be defined without a measure - only knowing the null sets. But I struggle tu understand how we obtain a measure to define $L^2(X,\mathcal{A}, \mu)$? Is it obtained somehow from predual of $L^\infty$ being $L^1$?
I would be grateful for some explanation.

title: Confusion regarding Adams spectral sequence and unoriented cobordism
text:
So this probably the simplest (and thus trivial) place to look at the Adams spectral sequence but I thought it would be good for understanding since I know what the unoriented cobordism ring should look like.
Via the Poyntragin Thom construction we know that the cobordism ring is $\pi_*(MO)$, i.e. $\bigoplus_n\pi_n(MO)$ where $\pi_n(MO)$ is the $n$th stable homotopy group of the Thom spectrum $MO(n)$. We want to use the Adams spectral sequence to calculate the homotopy groups. Let $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z[x_1,\dots]$ have grading $|x_i|=i$, then the $n$th stable homotopy group, should be the vector subspace of $(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb [x_1,\dots])_n$ with basis $$\{x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_k}:(i_1,\dots, i_k)\text{ is a non dyadic partition of $n$}\}$$
Now I have already shown that $H^*(MO)$ is a free module over the mod $2$ steenrod algebra $\mathfrak a_2$, so applying the Adams spectral sequence should be really very easy. Indeed, we have that:
\begin{align}
E_2^{s,t}=\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathfrak a_2}^s(H^t(MO),\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)
\end{align}
which is zero for all $s\geq 1$ because $H^*(MO)$ is free over $\mathfrak a_2$, so our spectral sequence stabilizes at the second page. For $s=0$ we have that $E_2^{0,t}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak a_2}(H^t(MO),\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z) $. Via the Thom isomorphism, we have that $$H^t(MO)\cong H^{t+k}(MO(k))\cong H^t(BO_k)\cong (\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z[x_1,\dots, x_k])_t$$
for all $k\geq t$.
I believe that the Adams spectral sequence now tells us that that $\pi_t(MO)\otimes \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak a_2}(H^t(MO),\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)$, but how do I conclude from this that $\pi_t(MO)$ is what it should be?
Thank you for the help.
Edit: It seems I messed up the internal grading, we should have:
$$E_2^{s,t}=\operatorname{Ext}_{\mathfrak a_2}^{s,t}(H^*(MO),\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)$$
where the $t$ grading is induced by $H^*(MO)$. Here since the only groups which stay alive are $\operatorname{Hom}$ groups, the $\operatorname{Hom}^t_{\mathfrak a_2}(H^*(MO),\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)$ is precisely the homomorphisms which have support contained in $H^n(MO)$.

title: Stochastic independence between two "symmetric" events
text:
Let $a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2}$ be four continuous i.i.d. random variables with support $[1,\bar{m}]$ and $1 \neq \bar{m}$. If needed, it can be assumed that they are all uniformly distributed on an interval $[1,\bar{m}]$, but I believe that it is not necessary to make use of their specific distribution. Let $A$ be the event $a_{1}a_{2} < b_{1}b_{2}$ and $B$ be the event $a_{1} + b_{1} \leq k_{1} \land a_{2} + b_{2} \leq k_{2}$, where $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ are arbitrary values from $(1,2\bar{m}]$ ($k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ should not be equal to the left boundary of the support of $a_{1} + b_{1}$ and $a_{2} + b_{2}$). The goal is to show that $A$ and $B$ are stochastically independent.
There is an intuition why this would be the case. The event $A$ by itself has probability $1/2$ irrespective of the specific distributions of the random variables. Now, let the original random variables be supported on $[1,2]$ and let $k_{1} = 2.5$ and $k_{2} = 3.5$. Then, if $B$ is fulfilled, the sum $a_{1} + b_{1}$ cannot exceed $2.5$ and the sum $a_{2} + b_{2}$ cannot exceed $3.5$. Yet, under those restrictions we still have "equally many" combinations of the original random variables such that $A$ is true and such that $A$ is not true. For instance, if the realisations are $a_{1} = 1.1, b_{1} = 1.2$ and $a_{2} = 2, b_{2} = 1.3$, the event $A$ is not fulfilled, but I can now swap around the values and get the realisations $a'_{1} = 1.2, b'_{1} = 1.1$ and $a'_{2} = 1.3, b'_{2} = 2$ for which $A$ is fulfilled. Therefore, for any values $k_{1}$ and $k_{1}$ of the event $B$, there is a one-to-one correspdonence between the space of the variables where $A$ is fulfilled and the space where $A$ is not fulfilled so that these sets are intuitively "equally large" and, given the overall symmetry of the arrangement, should carry the same probability. Accordingly, the probability of $A$ given $B$ should still be $1/2$, showing that the two events are independent.
Does anyone have an idea how one could formalise this intuition to turn it into a general argument or how to prove independence of the events in some other way? While independence of $A$ and $B$ seems intuitively true, I spent a whole week on trying to formalise and generalise the argument in a way that goes beyond just saying: "This is obviously true because of symmetry." Thanks in advance -- I am happy to mention any helper in the paper where this problem has relevance.

Assuming that this is correct (see derivation below), I was wondering:

Is there a name for this?
Is it useful in any way? For mathematics, computation, etc.


Suppose we have a division ring $(R,+,\cdot)$, with identity $\mathbf{0}$, unity $\mathbf{1}$, additive inverse of $x$ denoted as $-x$, and multiplicative inverse denoted as $x^{-1}$.
Define the elements of group $(G,\circ)$ as $\{f=[a_f,b_f], a_f\in R\setminus\mathbf{0},b_f\in R\}$.
The idea is that $f$ is a function $R\rightarrow R$ where $f(x):=a_f x + b_f$; the goal is to define $\circ:G\times G\rightarrow G$ such that we have function composition. We can do this by defining $f\circ g:=[a_f a_g,a_f b_g + b_f]$, i.e., $a_f(a_g x + b_g) + b_f=a_f a_g x + a_f b_g + b_f$.
The intuition is that we can compose any number of additions, subtractions, multiplications, and divisions and then apply them later. Sort of like computing bank account transactions and interest over time without knowing the starting balance.

Mutiplication by $x\neq\mathbf{0}$ would be $[x,\mathbf{0}]$.
Division by $x\neq\mathbf{0}$ would be $[x^{-1},\mathbf{0}]$.
Addition of $x$ would be $[\mathbf{1},x]$.
Subtraction of $x$ would be $[\mathbf{1},-x]$.


Proof that this is a group:

$[a,b]\circ[c,d]=[ac,ad+b]\in G$ because $ac\in R\setminus\mathbf{0}$ and $ad+b\in R$.

The identity for this group is $e:=[\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0}]$.

$[a,b]\circ[\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0}]=[a\mathbf{1},a\mathbf{0}+b]=[a,b]$
$[\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0}]\circ[a,b]=[\mathbf{1}a,\mathbf{1}b+\mathbf{0}]=[a,b]$


The inverse of $[a,b]$ can be defined as $[a^{-1},a^{-1}(-b)]$.

$[a,b]\circ[a^{-1},a^{-1}(-b)]=[aa^{-1},a(a^{-1}(-b))+b]=[\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0}]=e$
$[a^{-1},a^{-1}(-b)]\circ[a,b]=[a^{-1}a,a^{-1}b+a^{-1}(-b)]=[\mathbf{1},\mathbf{0}]=e$ (using distributive property of $R$)


Lastly, $\circ$ is associative.

$([a,b]\circ[c,d])\circ[e,f]=[ac,ad+b]\circ[e,f]=[(ac)e,(ac)f+(ad+b)]=[ace,acf+ad+b]$
$[a,b]\circ([c,d]\circ[e,f])=[a,b]\circ[ce,cf+d]=[a(ce),a(cf+d)+b]=[ace,acf+ad+b]$




Note that this doesn't depend on addition in $R$ being commutative, even though it's still required by definition of a ring.
I also think we could do this with a group $V$ and a group $M$ whose elements are endomorphisms of $V$ that distribute, with the derived group having elements in $M\times V$, and use the mostly same construction and proof above. (Proving closedness would be slightly more complicated.)

title: How many neighbourhoods are needed to cover the edge graph of a 6 dimensional hypercube
text:
For a vertex in a graph, define its neighbourhood to be the set containing itself and all its neighbours (sometimes referred to as closed neighbourhood to distinguish from just the set of neighbours).  So for example, in the graph formed from the $1$-skeleton of the $6$-dimensional hypercube, every neighbourhood has cardinality $7$.  Say a set of neighbourhoods covers a graph, if its union contains all the vertices of the graph.
Question How many neighbourhoods are needed to cover the edge graph of the $6$-dimensional hypercube?
I am particularly interested in whether the number is above $12$.  So far I have managed to get $12$ neighbourhoods which cover all but two of the vertices, so the minimal number of neighbourhoods is at most $14$.  We get a crude lower bound by dividing $64$ by $7$ and rounding up to $10$.
Taking a greedy approach, it is possible to select $8$ disjoint neighbourhoods, which then cover $56$ of the vertices.  However, no pair of the remaining $8$ vertices belong to a common neighbourhood, so this approach ends up needing $16$ neighbourhoods, which we have already beaten.
We may depict a $6$ dimensional hypercube as a chessboard, where squares are adjacent precisely when they are $4$ squares apart horizontally (or vertically), $2$ squares apart horizontally (or vertically), but in the same horizontal half (resp. vertical half), or $1$ square apart horizontally (or vertically), but in the same horizontal quarter (resp. vertical quarter).

title: Proof of a modified Perron-Frobenius theorem using complex analysis
text:
For context, the question I'm trying to solve (Q1 of this) asks us to prove a modified version of the Perron-Frobenius theorem using complex analysis. Let $A \neq 0$ be a $n \times n$ real matrix with non-negative entries. Let $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ in $\mathbb C$ be the (possibly repeated) eigenvalues of $A$ and $M = \max\{ |\lambda_1|, \dots, |\lambda_n|\}$. The goal is to show that $M$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.
The question asks us to consider the functions $F(z) = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{M}{M - \lambda_j z}$ and its Taylor series $f(z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k z^k$ around $0$. I've shown that
$$
c_k = \frac 1{M^k}(\lambda_1^k + \cdots + \lambda_n^k) = \frac 1{M^k}\mathrm{Tr}(A^k),
$$
and the radius of convergence of $f$ is $1$ (the trace bit tells us that $c_k$ is real and non-negative). The plan now is to show that $\sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k = \infty$, i.e. $f$ blows up at $z = 1$, which necessitates $F$ blows up at $z = 1$ (since $f$ and $F$ agree for $x$ real $\nearrow 1$), which means $M$ is an eigenvalue. Since $c_k\geq 0$, it suffices to show that $\sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k$ does not converge. Terms with eigenvalues of smaller modulus than $M$ clearly die when $k \to \infty$ due to the $M^k$ in the denominator, so let $\lambda_{j_1}, \dots, \lambda_{j_m}$ be the eigenvalues of modulus $M$, so let them be $Me^{i\theta_1}, \dots, Me^{i\theta_m}$. Then my intuition is that we can find infinitely many $n$ making
$$
|e^{in\theta_1} + \cdots + e^{in \theta_m}| > \frac12, \quad \text{say},
$$
by "simultaneously aligning the angles near an integer multiple of $2\pi$ using large $n$", then we'll have the result by the divergence test.
However, I have no idea how to show this. It feels somewhat similar in spirit to the density of integer multiples of an irrational number mod $1$ in $[0, 1)$ (e.g. this post), but the different terms interacting makes it trickier.

title: If $A,B\subset[1,n]$ and $|A|>\frac{n}{2}$, then is $|(2A-B)\cap [1,n]|\geq|B|$?
text:
Let $[1,n]=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$. For two subsets $A,B\subset [1,n]$, define $2A-B=\{2a-b|a\in A, b\in B\}$.

If $A,B\subset[1,n]$ and $|A|>\frac{n}{2}$, then is $|(2A-B)\cap [1,n]|\geq|B|$?

I have tried some example constructions and it seems that if $A,B\subset[1,n]$ and $|A|>\frac{n}{2}$, then $|(2A-B)\cap [1,n]|\geq|B|$.
However, I have found it hard to prove this. The classic lower bound of $|2A-B|\geq |A|+|B|-1$ does not account for how many terms are in $[1,n]$.
This would be tight, as if we take $A=[1,\frac{n}{4}]\cup[\frac{3n}{4}+1,n]$ and $B=[n-|B|+1,n]$ then $|A|=\frac{n}{2}$ and:

For $|B|\geq\frac{n}{2}+1$, you get $|(2A-B)\cap [1,n]|=|B|-2$

For $|B|=\frac{n}{2}$, you get $|(2A-B)\cap [1,n]|=|B|-1$


For the same $A$ and $B=[\frac{n}{2},\frac{n}{2}+1]$, we have $|(2A-B)\cap [1,n]|=0<|B|$.
Additionally, if you take $A=[1,\frac{n}{4}]\cup[\frac{3n}{4},n]$ and $B=[n-|B|+1,n]$, then $|A|=\frac{n}{2}+1$ and:

For $|B|\geq \frac{n}{2}+1$, you get $|(2A-B)\cap [1,n]|=|B|$

For $|B|\leq \frac{n}{2}$, you get $|(2A-B)\cap [1,n]|>|B|$

title: If $f:\mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ is monotone then it is Borel measurable
text:
This question has been posted several times, but I have not seen any proof match mine. I am following Folland's text, and was wondering if my proof was valid (inspired by Folland's proof that the sgn function is Borel measurable).
Note that since $f$ is monotonic, the points (denoted by $P$) at which it is discontinuous is at most countable. Let U be an open set in $\mathbb R$, so $f^{-1}(U) = \{ x \in \mathbb R : f(x) \in U \} = \{x \in P : f(x) \in U \}\cup \{x \in \mathbb R\setminus P : f(x) \in U \}$.
The former is some subset of the countable union of points $ \cup_{p \in P} \{p\}$ which is clearly a Borel set, and for the latter since $f$ is continuous on $R \setminus P$ we can easily show that $\{x \in R \setminus P : f(x) \in U\}$ is open and therefore a Borel set.

title: A Question about What's Wrong with My Computation of Polar Equation of a Hyperbola Centered at its Right Focus
text:
I am trying to compute the polar equation of a hyperbola which uses the right focus $F_2$ as the center of the coordinates, but the result I got is wrong. Here is my solution:

Given the euqation of a hyperbola:
$$\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$$
if we shift the center of the coordinates from the origin $(0,0)$ to the right focus $F_2: (c,0)=(\sqrt{a^2 + b^2},0)$, then the center of the hyperbola will be located to the left of the new origin $F_2$, so the new equation of the hyperbola is
$$\frac{(x+c)^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$$
which is equivalent to
$$\frac{(x+ae)^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{a^2(e^2 - 1)} = 1\tag{8.1.1}$$
where $e = \frac{c}{a} \in (1,+\infty)$ is the eccentricity of this hyperbola.
Then, let $P$ be an arbitrary point on the boundary of the hyperbola, $r>0$ be the distance from $P$ to $F_2$, and $\theta$ be the angle formed by $P, F_2$ and $x-$axis, and we have $P: (r \cos(\theta), r \sin(\theta).$ And then, plug what we have now into $(8.1.1)$, we get
\begin{align*}
&\qquad \frac{(r \cos(\theta)+ae)^2}{a^2} - \frac{r^2 \sin^2(\theta)}{a^2(e^2 - 1)} = 1\\
&\Rightarrow (e^2 \cos^2(\theta) - 1) r^2 + 2ae(e^2-1)\cos(\theta) r + a^2(e^2-1)^2 = 0\\
&\Rightarrow r = \frac{-2ae(e^2-1)\cos(\theta) \pm \sqrt{4a^2e^2(e^2-1)^2\cos^2(\theta) - 4a^2(e^2-1)^2 (e^2 \cos^2(\theta) - 1)} }{2(e^2 \cos^2(\theta) - 1)}
\end{align*}
Since $r>0$ and $e-1>0$, we have
\begin{align*}
r &= \frac{-2ae(e^2-1)\cos(\theta) + \sqrt{4a^2e^2(e^2-1)^2\cos^2(\theta) - 4a^2(e^2-1)^2 (e^2 \cos^2(\theta) - 1)} }{2(e^2 \cos^2(\theta) - 1)}\\
&= \frac{-2ae(e^2-1)\cos(\theta) + \sqrt{4a^2(e^2-1)^2} }{2(e^2 \cos^2(\theta) - 1)}\\
&= \frac{-2ae(e^2-1)\cos(\theta) + 2a(e^2-1) }{2(e^2 \cos^2(\theta) - 1)}\\
&= \frac{a(e^2-1)(1-e \cos(\theta)) }{e^2 \cos^2(\theta) - 1}\\
&= \frac{-a(e^2-1)}{1 + e \cos(\theta)}
\end{align*}
But when I check the answer key, the answer is $\frac{a(e^2-1)}{1 + e \cos(\theta)}$, which doesn't have the negative symbol.
So I am wondering where I made the mistake. Can somebody help check it and point out where the mistake is? Thanks!

title: Given a n-cube, why is it that in a net we can't have cycles in its facet-graph?
text:
Let's take it easier to visualize first, given a normal 3 dimensional cube in real life an cut along its edges (ridges more formally called) we can unfold it into the $xy$ plane if the cube was sitting on top of it. One way think to think of this is to think of the faces of the cube as a nodes and the connective edges between faces as edges in this new abstract graph. An unfolding is a subgraph such that it mustn't have any isolated nodes, otherwise there would be a totally cutoff face of the cube (that is to say that the graph is connected) and that there are no cycles of any size in it. So that means that an unfolding is a spanning tree of the graph of the cube.
In the general case, given an n-dimensional cube, construct the graph that represents its facets and the edges are its ridges, then an unfolding is a spanning tree of this graph.
My question: is this "no-cycle" rule necessary in higher dimension? Sure in 3 dimensional and even 2 dimensional cubes it makes sense that we need this but why would higher dimensional analogues need this condition too? Just because a rule seems beautifully nice to generalize doesn't mean that we should extrapolate with it. Couldn't it be possible to unfold, let's say, a 4-cube such that it contains cycles? Or a 10-cube having a 7-cycle in it can still be unfolded somehow into a lower dimension?

title: Twists of Holomorphic Forms by Principal Characters
text:
So I know that if $f \in \mathscr{M}_{k}(N,\chi)$ has Fourier expansion
$$f(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0}a(n)e^{2\pi inz},$$
and $\psi$ is a primitive character modulo $M$, then the twist
$$(f \otimes \psi)(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0}a(n)\psi(n)e^{2\pi inz}$$
lives in $\mathscr{M}_{k}(NM^{2},\chi\psi^{2})$. The proof essentially uses the primitivity of $\psi$ to write
$$\psi(n) = \frac{1}{\tau(\bar{\psi})}\sum_{r \pmod{M}}\bar{\psi}(r)e^{\frac{2\pi irn}{M}},$$
and from here you interchange sums etc. What I am curious about is if the primitivity of $\psi$ can be dropped. I've looked around the stack and it seems that this is possible (see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/158278/modular-form-on-gamma-0n). However, I am unsure how one would prove this. By multiplcativity of the characters you can assume $\psi$ is principal but then you can't use this sum trick above. In the case that the modulus is odd you could use squares of primitive quadratic characters given by the Jacobi symbol to get the result, but can you do better? It seems odd to exclude the case that $M$ is even since this generally doesn't cause issues for holomorphic forms (as far as I know).
Motivation for the question: In certain moment problems one studies the family $\{L(s,f \otimes \psi)\}_{\psi \pmod{M}}$. But for all of these $L$-functions to have nice properties such as analytic continuation, functional equation, etc. we need $f \otimes \psi$ to be a holomorphic form. This is clear if $\psi$ is primitive but it is not clear if $\psi$ is induced.

title: Using the Euler class to show that $\mathbb {CP}^4$ does not embed in $\mathbb R^{12}$
text:
Using the definition of the Euler class I am trying to prove then that $\mathbb {CP}^4$ cannot be embedded in $\mathbb R^{12}$. I know that the are other ways to do this in more generality, but they use advanced technology that I don't have, this is supposed to be doable using only the definition of the Euler class and possible any of the following facts that I have already proven:

For the tautological line bundle $L = L_{\mathbb{CP}^n}$ over $\mathbb{CP}^n$, $a := -c_1(L) \in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^n)$,

$$T(\mathbb{CP}^n) \oplus \mathbb{C} \cong L^* \oplus \cdots \oplus L^* \quad (\text{$n+1$ copies}).$$

The Chern classes of $T(\mathbb{CP}^n)$ and the Pontryagin classes of the real vector bundle are:
$$c(T(\mathbb{CP}^n)) = (1 + a)^{n+1}, \quad p(T(\mathbb{CP}^n)) = (1 + a^2)^{n+1}.$$

Try: I know that for any real oriented vector bundle $E$ over $M$ of rank $ r$, the Euler class is a cohomology class $e(E) \in H^r(M)$. Considering even-dimensional vector bundles to avoid triviality: $r = 2l$
For a real oriented vector bundle $E$, it is related to the Pontryagin class by: $p_l(E) = e(E)^2$.
I also know that the total Pontryagin class of $T(\mathbb{CP}^4)$ is:
$$
p(T(\mathbb{CP}^4)) = (1 + a^2)^5,
$$
where $a = -c_1(L) \in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^4, \mathbb{Z})$. Expanding this, we find, since $a^5=0$:
$$
p(T(\mathbb{CP}^4)) = 1 + 5a^2 + 10a^4 + 10a^6 + 5a^8 + a^{10}=1 + 5a^2 + 10a^4.
$$
Assume that $ \mathbb{CP}^4 $ embeds into $ \mathbb{R}^{12}$. Then the tangent bundle and the normal bundle satisfy:
$$
T(\mathbb{CP}^4) \oplus N \cong \mathbb{R}^{12},
$$
The cohomology ring of $ \mathbb{CP}^4 $ is:
$$
H^*(\mathbb{CP}^4, \mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}[a] / (a^5),
$$
where $ a \in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^4, \mathbb{Z}) $. This means:

The highest nonzero cohomology group is $ H^8(\mathbb{CP}^4, \mathbb{Z})$, generated by $a^4$.
Any term of degree higher than $8$, such as $a^6$ or $a^8$, must vanish.

Using the Whitney product formula for Pontryagin classes:
$$
1=p(\mathbb{R}^{12})=p(T(\mathbb{CP}^4)) \cdot p(N) ,
$$
where $ p(\mathbb{R}^{12}) = 1 $ because $ \mathbb{R}^{12} $ is trivial.
Let the total Pontryagin class of $ N $ be: $p(N) = 1 + p_1(N) + p_2(N).$
Substituting $ p(T(\mathbb{CP}^4)) = 1 + 5a^2 + 10a^4  $, we get:
$$
(1 + 5a^2 + 10a^4 ) \cdot (1 + p_1(N) + p_2(N)) = 1.
$$
$$
1 + p_1(N) + p_2(N) + 5a^2 + 5a^2 \cdot p_1(N) + 5a^2 \cdot p_2(N) + 10a^4 + 10a^4 \cdot p_1(N) + 10a^4 \cdot p_2(N) =1
$$
The rank of $ N $ is $r=4$, so its Euler class $ e(N) $ lies in $ H^4(\mathbb{CP}^4, \mathbb{Z}) $, which is generated by $ a^2 $.
so $e(N) = ka^2$ for some integer $k$.
By the relation between Pontryagin classes and the Euler class $p_2(N) = e(N)^2$. Substituting $e(N)$, we get: $p_2(N) = (ka^2)^2 = k^2a^4$, so $p_2(N)$ has degree $8$.
Since $p_1(N)$ has degree $4$ by definition of Pontryagin classes, $p_1(N)=ma^2$.
Equating terms of degree 4
$$
 5a^2 + p_1(N) = 0. \tag{1'} 
$$
Then $m=-5$ and  $p_1(N)=-5a^2$.
Equating terms of degree $8$ and substituting  $p_1(N)=-5a^2$ and $p_2(N)=k^2a^4$:
$$
0 =10a^4 + 5a^2 \cdot p_1(N) + p_2(N) =10a^4 + 5a^2 \cdot (-5a^2) + k^2a^4. \tag{1}
$$
from which $k^2a^4=15a^4$ ie $k^2=15$ since  $a^4$ is a generator of $H^8(\mathbb{CP}^4,\mathbb{Z})\cong \mathbb{Z}$, so it is not $0$.
As sanity check:
Equating terms of degree 12 :
$$
5a^2 \cdot p_2(N)  + 10a^4 \cdot p_1(N)  = 0. \tag{1''}
$$
we get $-35a^6=0$ which is true
Equating terms of degree 16 :
$$
10a^4 \cdot p_2(N)  = 0. \tag{1'''}
$$
we get $150a^8=0$ which is also true
This shows that the Whitney product formula cannot be satisfied under the assumption that $\mathbb{CP}^4 $ embeds into $ \mathbb{R}^{12} $.
Is this a valid proof? Otherwise how would you proceed?

title: understanding the concept of "least squares" in linear algebra
text:
I'm studying orthogonality in linear algebra, but am struggling to grasp the "least" part of least squares.  I get that when you have a vector $b$ that falls outside $C(A)$, there is no solution vector $x$ such that $Ax=b$.  However, $b$ will lie somewhere in $\Bbb{R^m}$ and its location must be in $N(A^T)$ since $C(A)$ and $N(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements and together, they span all of $\Bbb{R^m}$
It makes intuitive sense that the least distance from $b$ to $C(A)$ will be a vector $e$ that is perpendicular to $C(A)$ and meets $C(A)$ at the point $A\hat{x}$, forming a right triangle with hypotenuse $b$, such that $\Vert{b}\Vert^2=\Vert{e}\Vert^2+\Vert{A\hat{x}}\Vert^2$
So, I assume this last equation is where the idea of least squares come from, but I don't see any other option for "squares" that would produce a larger $e$.  If I choose any other vector $x$, except for $\hat{x}$, $e$ will no longer be perpendicular to $C(A)$ making $\Vert{b}\Vert^2=\Vert{e}\Vert^2+\Vert{Ax}\Vert^2$ untrue. If $Ax$ is shorter, $e$ will be shorter, but $b$ would be different.
It seems, in this context, that a better descriptive term would be the "only square" rather than "least squares". What am I missing here?

Our whole stack of disks is on left most rod and our objective is to find the smallest no. of steps to transfer it to the right most rod.

Now put the stack on the right most disk on the left most disk using the procedure of the indistinguishable disks, leading to another reversal which leads to our original configuration. Now we put all the disks on the middle rod on the right most rod, which leads to them now being in original configuration. Finally, what we do is that we take all the disks on the left most rod and put them on the right most rod but with the procedure to mantain the same configuration, as right now the configuration is the same as original.


  
This implies $b_k=2a_{k-1}+2n_k+b_{k-1}$. And from solving this I got $b_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}2^{n-k+1}n_k-1$.
Am I correct, is this the shortest way, I have made some arguements to convince myself but I have yet to confirm?

title: A curve with corners is not a submanifold
text:
Consider the graph of the absolute value function as a curve on the plane. It is intuitively clear that the origin is a "singular" point, and that this prevents this curve from being an immersed submanifold of the plane.
How can this fact be properly stated and proved?
(in the general case, and not just for the absolute value graph).
For example, in the study of algebraic curves one can define a singularity by looking at the intersection multiplicity of the curve with lines.
In differential geometry we know that, if a subset $C$ of $\mathbb R^n$ is given as the zero locus of a function $F$ and a point $p$ on $C$ is regular (i.e. the differential of $F$ at $p$ is surjective), then $p$ has a neighbourhood whose intersection with $C$ is a smooth embedded submanifold. However, if the point is critical, we can't conclude that there is a "true" singularity. For example the function $F(x,y)=x^2$ defines a perfectly well embedded submanifold, but every point is critical for the function $F$. Hence, how can we give a meaningful definition (maybe restricted to some specific class of cases) of what I called a singularity?
It seems to me that (restrincting for simplicity to the case of curves) in order to give a definition of singular point on a curve we should first define what a curve is. The straightforward definition as a 1-dimensional submanifold doesn't work, because in this case there would not be any singular point. Hence a more useful possibility could be through a parametrization. However, if we then use a parametrization to define, e.g., the notion of a singular point, then we have to show that it is independent on the chosen parametrization.
Following this route I've arrived to the following conjecture, which is about a specific case (curve with corners). I would like to know whether it is true and, apart from proving or disproving it, how to deal with this general problem.
Consider a piecewise regular curve in $\mathbb R^n$, i.e. a continuous function $r\colon (a,b)\to \mathbb R^n$ and a subdivision $a=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_m=b$ such that the restriction of $r$ to $[t_i,t_{i+1}]$ is a smooth function with nonvanishing derivative. Assume moreover that right and left limits of the derivative are finite at the points $t_i$ and that $r$ is a homeomorphism onto its image. We say that there is a corner at the point $p=r(t_i)$ if the limits $$c_i^+:=\lim_{t\to t_i ^+} r'(t)$$ and $$c_i^-:=\lim_{t\to t_i ^-} r'(t)$$ are such that $c_i^+\neq\lambda c_i^-$ for any $\lambda>0$.
Conjecture: If the curve $r$ has a corner, then its image is not an immersed sumbanifold of $\mathbb R^n$.
In order to show this, it should be sufficient to prove that, if $p=r(t_i)$ is a corner, there isn't any smooth function $\phi\colon (-\epsilon,\epsilon)\to \mathbb R^n$ taking values in the image of $r$ and such that

$\phi'(t)\neq 0$ for all $t\in (-\epsilon,\epsilon)$
$\phi(0)=p$ is the corner.

This last statement encodes in some sense the parametrization invariance of the "corner", meaning that any other parametrization must have the corner and cannot hence be smooth.
However I can't find an easy way to prove it. I'd appreciate if someone could help me.

title: Does Calcium Sulfide Emit UV Light via Phosphorescence?

In this presentation by Niewenglowski at the French academy of science in 1896, there is a report of a photographic plate being darkened after being next to calcium sulfide that was exposed to sunlight. This is one of the papers that Henri Becquerel mentions as his inspiration for the experiment that led him to discover radioactivity.
Since the paper is in French, here is my translation of the beginning of it:

I noticed that phosphorescent bodies have similar properties towards sunlight as zinc sulfide has with Röntgen rays as they make them able to go through some bodies that would absorb them, a property that M. Charles Henry reported on during last session:
An ordinary photographic plate being wrapped in several sheets of black or red paper, I placed two coins on top, and I covered one of the half with a glass plate covered with phosphorescent powder (calcium sulfide) ; after four to five hours in sunlight, the half that had received direct sunlight was intact and bore no traces of the coin on top of it, showing that light did not go through the red or black paper ; the half that was receiving sunlight through the phosphorescent plate had become completely black, except for the part corresponding to the coin, creating a white-on-black silhouette.

I am a bit surprised by this result: at that time everybody was experimenting with X rays, and X rays can go through dark paper, but how can you produce X rays with just sunlight?
Later in the same paper, Niewenglowski mentions the possibility of pressure causing artefacts in this type of experiments, as in if the coin presses against the photographic plate it could cause an imprimpt, but he seems to say he was very careful about avoiding this.
So I was thinking maybe calcium sulfide emits UV light through phosphorescence? And maybe the black paper that Niewenglowski used maybe was opaque to visible light but not to the exact wavelength produced by the phosphorecent calcium sulfide.

title: Pressure of mixture after mixing

As $P_{m,2} = P_{i,2} = 200 \,\text{kPa}$. It is obvious that the entropy change is independent of the composition of the mixture in this case and that it depends on only the mole fraction of the gases of the mixture.

As you can see from the answer, they assumed that after the partition has been removed, the mixture pressure $p_{m,2}$ is exactly the same as the individual pressures $p_{\mathrm{O}_2,1}$ and $p_{\mathrm{CO}_2,1}$ before the partition was removed.

title: What's the easiest way to get the speed at the tip of a double pendulum?
text:
Say we have a double pendulum consisting of two rods of lengths $l_1$ and $l_2$, anchored at points $p_1$ and $p_2$ respectively (hence $p_2$ is time-variant), where the first rod is at an angle $\theta_1$ from the vertical, and the second rod is at an angle $\theta_2$ from the first rod, and the corresponding angular velocities are $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$.  Now we want the speed (squared) at the tip of the second rod to plug into the Lagrangian.  If we do everything in Cartesian coordinates, we have to get the position vector at the tip in terms of both angles, differentiate it to get velocity, and apply Pythagoras to get speed squared.  The algebra turns out to be very tedious and redundant.
An easier way is to note that the tip has a separate velocity component due to each angle, that is,
$$\vec v = \frac{\partial\vec r}{\partial\theta_1}\omega_1 + \frac{\partial\vec r}{\partial\theta_2}\omega_2 \equiv \vec v_1 + \vec v_2$$
where $\vec r$ and $\vec v$ are the position and velocity of the tip relative to the anchor.  These two terms are really just the tangential velocities of the circular motions of the tip about $p_1$ and $p_2$, and thus have magnitudes of $r\omega_1$ and $l_2\omega_2$, with $r$ the magnitude of $\vec r$.  Furthermore, as each velocity is perpendicular to its corresponding radius, the angle between them is the same as that between $\vec r$ and the second rod, which we can call $\alpha$.  Given all this, we apply the law of cosines three times: once on the triangle consisting of $l_1$, $l_2$, and $r$ to find $r$, again on the same triangle to find $\cos{\alpha}$, and finally on the triangle represented by the equation $\vec v_1 + \vec v_2 = \vec v$ to get $v^2$, since the angle there is $\pi-\alpha$.
This seems algebraically much neater, but I still have the impression there's a bit of redundancy here; it left me with the feeling there should be an even simpler, more elegant approach, so I'm reaching out to see if anyone has one.

title: Physical interpretation of the Green's function approach to Laplace equation
text:
Consider the Laplace equation in a region $D$ with boundary $\partial D$,
$$
\nabla^2 u = 0, \qquad u|_{\partial D} = \varphi \ .
$$

In terms of electrostatic field, we are computing the interior potential by knowing the boundary potential; the boundary potential will create some physical surface charge density $\rho_0(\mathbf{r}')$ at $\mathbf{r}' \in \partial D$.

The Green's function approach first constructs $G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_0)$ such that
$$
\nabla^2_\mathbf{r} G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_0) = - \delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0), \qquad
G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_0)|_{\mathbf{r} \in \partial D} = 0 \ .
$$
The final solution will be
$$
u(\mathbf{r} \in D) = - \int_{\partial D} \varphi(\mathbf{r}') \frac{\partial G(\mathbf{r}', \mathbf{r})}{\partial n'} d\sigma' \ .
$$
Here, $\mathbf{r}' \in \partial D$ is the integration variable, $d\sigma'$ denotes the area element of $\partial D$.
I am struggling to understand the physics in the result. Assume $u$ to be the electric potential.
The $G(\mathbf{r}', \mathbf{r})$ is simply the electric potential at $\mathbf{r}' \in \partial D$ from a point charge sitting at $\mathbf{r}$ (surrounded by grounded conductor at $\partial D$, carrying some induced surface charges). The derivative $\partial G(\mathbf{r}', \mathbf{r})/\partial n'$ computes the corresponding normal electric field, propotional to the induced surface charge density $\rho_\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{r}')$. So the potential roughly is
$$
- \int_{\partial D} \varphi(\mathbf{r}')\rho_\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{r}')d\sigma' \ .
$$
This looks weird: why is the interior potential be $\sim$ boundary potential $\times$ induced charge density?
As pointed out in a comment in a related question link, Jackson has some discussions pointing out that the surface term should be interpreted as from a dipole layer $D = - \epsilon_0 u$. Where is this dipole layer from?

title: Apple falling from boat mast
text:
To better understand how gravity and movement works, a common question is to ask where an apple would land if dropped from the top of a mast on a moving boat (let's assume a boat with a motor but with a mast, and no wind blowing apart from the relative speed of the boat, and a constant speed, let's say 50km/h, it's a fast boat).
People often mistakenly answer it would land on the rear of the boat, because the boat is still advancing forward while the apple is falling straight down.
So it is explained that there is a conservation of movement, and the apple was moving at the same speed as the boat, and hence it would land at the base of the mast, and it is often added that it's the same case as if you jump on a moving train, you don't end up at the rear of the train, but instead land where you were before.
However it seems to me that those 2 examples are not the same. On a train, the compartment is closed, so the air is trapped and also moves with the train. With the boat case, there is no close environment, so as soon as it gets dropped, it loses contact with the boat and stops being accelerated by the boat motors (that counteract the water/air slowing it down, so that it maintains a constant speed), so starts being slowed down by the air around it.
Assuming a 20m mast, I think it takes roughly 2s for the apple to reach the boat, and I'd say that in 2s, the air has ample time to slow the apple enough so that it doesn't fall on the bottom of the mast, but rather closer to the rear of the boat. Am I wrong? How far would the apple land (if there's not enough numerical values, feel free to take any reasonable choice)?

title: What is the physical meaning of BFV action in BFV formalism?
text:
BFV formalism is the Hamiltonian counterpart of the Batalin-Vilkovisky (BV) formalism. Suppose we have a BV field theory
$$
(F, \omega, Q, S)
$$
which satisfies the variational formula with boundary:
$$
\delta S = \iota_Q\omega + \pi^*(\alpha)
$$
we can define BFV theory by:
$$
F^\partial = (F|_{\partial M}) / \ker(\delta \alpha)
\\
\omega^\partial = \delta\alpha
\\
\delta S^\partial = \iota_{Q^\partial}\omega^\partial
$$
Then $S^\partial$ is called the BFV action.
The question is, what is the physical meaning of $S^\partial$?
For example, in (first order) Maxwell theory, we have
$$
S = \int B dA + \frac{1}{2} B\star B + A^+dc
\\
S^\partial = \int c dB
$$
and in (first order) Yang-Mills theory we have
$$
S = \int BF_A + \frac{1}{2}B\star B + \frac{1}{2}\langle c,[c,c]\rangle + A^+(dc+[A,c]) + B^+[B,c]
\\
S^\partial = \int B (dc+[A,c]) + \frac{1}{2}A^+[c,c].
$$
For my guess, I think BFV is equivalent somehow to Hamiltonian BRST introduced in “quantization of gauge system” by Henneaux & Teitelboim and $S^\partial$ corresponds to Hamiltonian BRST operator $Q_{BRST}$.
Pros:

In quantization we quantize $S^\partial$ to $\Omega^\partial$ and then define physical states as $H^0(\Omega^\partial)$. This is the same story that we define physical states as $H^0(Q_{BRST})$ in Hamiltonian BRST.

Cons:

The spaces $F^\partial$ is not the extended phase space $P_{ext}$ in Hamiltonian BRST.
$$
F^\partial = \langle \phi , c, \phi^+, c^+, \dot{\phi}, \dot{c}, \dot{\phi^+} , \dot{c^+}\rangle|_{\partial M} / null
\\
P_{ext} = \langle \phi, c, P_\phi, P_c\rangle|_{\partial M}
$$
where $\phi$ denotes original fields and $c$ the ghost fields. So they are not equal and 2 times larger.
